Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

Couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

Minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

**Difficulty Rating: Hard — But for Specific, Solvable Reasons** This isn't hard because the booking process itself is complicated. Flyingblue.com is a functional, English-language booking tool that anyone can navigate. It's hard because of **timing and availability** — two factors that reward the prepared and punish the passive. **What Specifically Makes This Hard:** 1. **Monthly availability windows are brief.** You have 24–48 hours from the Promo announcement to act before the best dates disappear. If you're not watching, you miss the cycle entirely and wait another month. 2. **Dynamic pricing outside of Promo is punishing.** If you miss the Promo window and try to book a standard award on the same route, you could pay 2–3x more miles. The program's value is almost entirely concentrated in the monthly Promo structure. 3. **Coordination across accounts takes discipline.** Keeping 40,000–80,000 points liquid in a transferable account, not spending them on something else, and being ready to move instantly requires real points discipline. **Three Tips to Overcome the Challenge:** - **Automate your awareness.** Sign up for Flying Blue emails and follow deal-tracking communities so the announcement comes to you. - **Keep your points liquid in Chase or Amex.** The instant transfer speeds are your competitive advantage over slower-moving transfer paths. - **Be route-flexible, not date-flexible.** You may not get Paris in July, but you might get Amsterdam in September — and that's still an extraordinary redemption. If you're willing to build the habit of checking on the 1st of each month and keeping a points buffer ready, the hard part becomes routine. The ChooseFI community has proven this works — repeatedly.

Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com and enable email notifications. Keep at least 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in your Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt account. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.

Visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

Use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates quickly.

Transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

Promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. A business class transatlantic award that normally costs 80,000 to 100,000 miles one-way can drop to 40,000 to 50,000 miles on a Promo Reward. Additionally, fuel surcharges are eliminated on promo awards, saving another $100 to $300 per ticket that would otherwise be charged on standard awards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards and Citi ThankYou are the best because they transfer instantly to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

Yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

The best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Keep 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in reserve, check on the 1st of every month, and book the moment you find a route that matches your travel list. Over time, this single strategy can deliver thousands of dollars in business class experiences at economy-level points costs.

#8445. Fractional Shares Let You Invest by the Dollar – but Switching Brokers Sells Them

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. With fractional shares, every dollar of a small deposit is invested at once instead of waiting in cash for a whole share. Set up automatic monthly buys of one broad index fund at a fractional-share broker, and expect the fractions to be sold, not transferred, if you switch brokers.

At $50 a month, buying only whole shares means a year of saving before you own one share of a $600 exchange-traded fund (ETF), a fund that trades like a stock. Fractions let each $50 buy about 0.083 of a share right away.

Which stocks and ETFs you can buy in fractions depends on the broker. Fidelity sells fractions of most stocks and ETFs listed on the NYSE or Nasdaq, from $1. J.P. Morgan Self-Directed Investing limits them to stocks in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes and the ETFs on its eligible list, from $5. Vanguard sells them on its own ETFs, from $1.

The catch that costs money comes when you move your account. FINRA, the regulator that oversees brokers, says fractional shares can’t transfer to another firm, so only your whole shares move and the fractions are sold for cash. In a regular brokerage account, unlike an IRA, that sale can mean tax on any gain.

Fractions have smaller drawbacks too. Fidelity gives them no shareholder vote, and fractional orders often go through only during regular market hours. Some brokers also collect a day’s fractional orders from all their customers and send them to the market together, which can change the price you pay. None of that hurts the best use of fractions, which is automatic dollar-amount buys of one broad index ETF you hold for years.

Your fractions add up to whole shares as you keep buying, so moving your account never sells more than one share’s worth of each fund you hold.

To find a broker that sells fractions of the ETF you want, compare the best brokers for fractional share investing.

Let’s face it, when you hear something like that, your first thought is, “This has got to be too good to be true.”

That was my initial reaction too. A free, do-it-all software that doesn’t suck? Highly doubtful.

But here’s the shocker: Systeme.io isn’t just blowing smoke. It’s a game-changer. As someone who’s navigated the maze of digital marketing tools, I was prepared for disappointment. Yet, Systeme.io left me floored with its capabilities.

Take it from someone who’s been around the block with the likes of ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp. These giants lure you in with free offerings, only to tighten the screws when your audience grows. Then there’s WordPress.org – great for setting up a blog, but it’s like climbing Everest if you’re a newbie.

Systeme.io, on the other hand, is a beast of a different nature. Offering highly effective landing pages and robust sales funnels with professional templates for free? That’s unheard of. It’s like stumbling upon a treasure chest in your backyard.

My first foray into landing page software was with ClickFunnels, an undeniably powerful tool. But once the 14-day trial evaporates, you’re staring down the barrel of a $100 monthly fee. Worth it if you’re a pro, but a gut punch for beginners.

Yes, you can test it out 100% completely FREE.

Absolutely. It’s a diamond in the rough, especially for those just starting their digital marketing journey. For the veterans, it might not have the same allure, but for the rookies, it’s a godsend. Forget the skepticism; Systeme.io is a disruptor that’s here to stay.

The platform serves a multifaceted purpose, aiming to simplify the digital marketing process. It’s designed for entrepreneurs and businesses seeking an integrated solution for email marketing, sales funnels, website building, and more.

The saving grace here is their tutorials. These are goldmines for beginners. They walk you through the process, breaking down what could be an overwhelming experience into manageable chunks. So, while the interface might not win any beauty contests, the support system in place is BIG help.

At the core of Systeme.io are several key features that make it a comprehensive digital marketing solution. These include email marketing capabilities, sales funnel creation tools, a website builder, options for hosting membership sites, and affiliate program management.

Each of these features is designed to work seamlessly with the others, providing a unified experience. The all-in-one nature of Systeme.io is its hallmark. It consolidates various marketing tools into one cohesive platform. This integration means you can manage email campaigns, build sales funnels, create websites, and even run affiliate programs without having to switch between different software. For many users, this integration simplifies the digital marketing process significantly, allowing for a more streamlined workflow.

However, it’s important to recognize that while Systeme.io covers a broad spectrum of functionalities, it may not offer the same depth as specialized standalone tools in each specific area.

These resources are designed to help users navigate through the initial complexity and make the most out of the platform’s features.

#8442. Give Each Goal the Account Built for It – 401(k), IRA, HSA, 529 & Brokerage

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Pick the investment account by what the money is for, because the account decides how it’s taxed and when you can withdraw it. Use a 401(k) or IRA for retirement, a health savings account for medical bills, a 529 plan for education, and a taxable brokerage account for other long-term goals.

Pick the wrong one and it costs you later, in tax you could have avoided or a penalty for taking money out early.

A traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account (IRA) can cut your taxable income now, and you pay income tax on withdrawals in retirement. A Roth 401(k) or IRA does the reverse. You pay tax on what goes in, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. Choosing between a Roth and a traditional IRA comes down to whether you expect a higher tax rate now or in retirement. You can put in up to $24,500 a year in a 401(k) and $7,500 across your traditional and Roth IRAs combined, with higher limits from age 50. Most withdrawals before age 59½ also cost a 10% penalty on top of any income tax.

A health savings account (HSA) is tax-free going in, while it grows, and coming out for qualified medical expenses. You can fund one only while you’re covered by an HSA-eligible health plan, such as one with a high deductible. A 529 plan grows tax-free and pays out tax-free for college and other qualified school costs, though what you put in isn’t deductible on your federal return. A taxable brokerage account has no tax break, but also no limits or withdrawal rules. You pay tax on its dividends each year and on gains when you sell.

You don’t need all five at once. Fill them in this order: your 401(k) up to any match your employer offers, then a Roth IRA or an HSA, then more 401(k) or a taxable account. A full financial order of operations also places debt payoff and an emergency fund among those steps.

A 28-year-old with no 401(k) who’s saving for retirement and for a down payment in four years needs two places, a Roth IRA for retirement and a high-yield savings account for the down payment.

Money you’ll need within about five years belongs in savings, not stocks, because a market drop right before you spend it could leave you short.

#8440. Free Stock Is Real Money – Use It to Break a Tie Between Brokers

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. Free stock from a broker is real money, but a sign-up share is often worth a few dollars. The broker you pick may hold your investments for decades. Shortlist online brokers by their costs, the funds they sell, and the account you need, then take a free-stock offer only from a broker on your shortlist.

A sign-up share pays you once. The broker’s fees and choice of funds affect you every year you stay, and any charge for moving your account out comes due the day you leave.

You can get free stock four ways. Brokers give shares to new customers who open or fund an account, as Webull’s free-share offer does, and to current customers who refer friends. Stash’s Stock-Back debit card pays rewards in stock, and Acorns invests the rewards you earn shopping with its partner brands.

The shares tend to be small, and they come with conditions. Robinhood’s sign-up stock is worth $5 to $200, and about 99% of new customers get the minimum. You can sell the share after 3 trading days, but you can’t withdraw its cash value for 60 days. It also comes only with an individual taxable account, not an individual retirement account (IRA). Any tax on it is yours, and its value may show up on a 1099 tax form.

Skipping that order can turn a free share into a loss. Say you take an $8 share from a broker that doesn’t carry the funds you want and charges $75 to transfer an account out. Paying the fee to move the account leaves you $67 behind. A fractional free share, a slice of one share, can’t transfer to another broker, the brokerage regulator FINRA notes, so you’d have to sell it first.

Take a free share only from a broker you’d have opened without it.

Find that broker among the best online brokers for beginners.

#8438. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Reduce your tax liability with the 50-20-0% rule for FMV

Mr. Money Mustache October 9, 2025, 1:55 pm

Excellent! Thanks JB – this is so useful that I will have to edit the article to include a link to that discussion on Reddit. For anyone reading it here: https://www.reddit.com/r/AmazonVine/comments/1iq0gze/reduce_your_tax_liability_with_the_50200_rule_for/

After you review every product, it’s is now a USED product and the FMV is greatly reduced. Remember we are all opening and using the products to review them

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

Using this rule, let’s say you bought $1000 worth of non branded stuff, you’d reduce FMV by $800. As the remaining resale value of the used products is now $200 using the 20% rule. You’d patties on $200, not $1000.

Edit: You are welcome to claim Amazon’s reported ETV as hobby income. Just remember:

To maintain access to vine, we are required to “do work” (aka review 60%+ of products) to get access to the products. The process of reviewing an item, results in an adjustment to the fair market value after doing so. After you review the item, the “remaining” value is not the inflated ETV.

If you don’t understand accounting, you need to be very detailed with your CPA. If you can’t be bothered with some simple accounting, you are welcome to pay your marginal tax rate for your ETV as hobby income.

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.

#8436. Investing in Your 20s – Take the Match, Open a Roth IRA, and Own Stocks

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Money you invest in your 20s has about 40 years to grow, so small amounts go far. Contribute enough to your 401(k) to get the full employer match, open a Roth IRA while your tax rate is low, and invest both accounts mostly in stocks through a target-date or broad stock index fund.

Starting early can matter more than the amount you put in, since money you invest at 25 gets 10 more years to compound than money you invest at 35.

A Roth IRA suits your 20s. You pay income tax on what you put in at today’s rate, and in retirement the money and its growth come out tax-free. That trade pays off most when your tax rate is low, and on a first salary it’s likely the lowest it will be in your career.

With about 40 years until retirement, you can hold mostly stocks, which swing more than bonds but have historically grown more. If the market drops 30% when you’re 25, every contribution buys shares for 30% less while prices stay down, and you won’t need to sell for decades. Keep buying through it.

Take the steps in this order. First, get the full match, the money your employer adds when you contribute, as soon as your plan allows. Build a starter emergency fund, a small cash cushion for surprise bills, at the same time. Next, pay off any high-interest debt, such as a credit card balance. Then, if your income is under the IRS’s ceiling for Roth contributions, open a Roth IRA and contribute up to the yearly limit, $7,500. Anything past that goes back into your 401(k).

In both accounts, pick a low-cost target-date fund named for the year you plan to retire. It holds mostly stocks while that year is far off and shifts toward bonds as it nears. A broad stock index fund, which owns small slices of hundreds or thousands of companies, works too.

At a hypothetical 7% average annual return, raising your contributions from 6% to 10% of a $50,000 salary adds $2,000 a year that grows to about $400,000 over 40 years. So each time your pay goes up, save another 1% or 2% of it until you and your employer together put in 15% of your pay.

Picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

The best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:

Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is honest. It earns that designation from three compounding challenges, not just one. **Challenge 1: Finding availability on multiple segments simultaneously.** Business class award space on popular long-haul routes is limited. Finding saver-level availability on one segment is manageable. Finding it on two connected segments, with dates that create a coherent stopover itinerary, requires persistence and flexibility. This is the primary barrier. **Challenge 2: Understanding Aeroplan's routing logic.** Aeroplan's stopover rules, multi-city booking interface, and the distinction between how partner awards are priced require more than surface-level familiarity with the program. A misunderstanding of how the stopover is added can result in a significantly higher points cost or a booking that doesn't reflect your intended itinerary. **Challenge 3: Coordinating the transfer timing.** With a 355-day booking window and fast-moving business class availability, the timing of your point transfers requires active management — particularly if you're not using Chase's instant transfer speed. ## Three Tips to Overcome These Challenges 1. **Start your availability research 60–90 days before the 355-day window opens.** Know your target route, your preferred stopover city, and your date range before you ever log into aeroplan.com. Preparation turns a chaotic search into a focused one. 2. **Use united.com as your availability research tool.** It searches the Star Alliance network and shows you realistic inventory without requiring you to commit points. 3. **Don't be discouraged by the learning curve.** Every hard redemption in the ChooseFI community gets easier the second time. Plenty of members who now book these routinely considered them impossible the first time they looked. The complexity is real — but so is the $10,000 of value sitting on the other side of it.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

Under the federal ability-to-pay rule, a card issuer has to weigh your income or assets against your current debts before it opens an account or raises your credit line. #8433. Reading a Stock Quote – You Buy at the Ask, Not the Last Price

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. This compensation may influence how and where offers appear on the site, including the order in which they appear on category pages. It does not influence our evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We do not include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

You buy at a stock quote’s ask, the lowest price a seller will take, and sell at its bid, the highest a buyer will pay. The gap between them costs you the moment you buy, and it’s usually widest on stocks that trade few shares. When it’s wide, use a limit order to set the most you’ll pay.

The big number on the quote is the last price, what the most recent trade paid. Your order won’t necessarily get it.

Say a stock last traded at $10.20 and is quoted at $10.00 bid and $10.40 ask. A market order, which buys at once at the best price available, pays about $10.40. Sell right back for about $10.00 and you’ve lost 40 cents a share, almost 4% of what you paid.

On a large company’s stock or a popular exchange-traded fund, that gap, called the spread, is often a penny during regular trading hours, a tiny fraction of the price. Low volume, meaning few shares trade each day, leaves fewer buyers and sellers competing on price, so the gap is wider.

Use a limit order on any stock with a wide gap, since a market order bigger than the ask size can buy the rest at higher prices. At the open and after hours, use one on every stock. An overnight market order usually goes through at the opening price, which can be far from the last price you saw. After hours, the Securities and Exchange Commission says the gap usually widens and many brokers accept only limit orders.

Set your limit no higher than the ask on the quote, so you never pay more than that price.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#8430. In Your 30s, Save 15% for Retirement – Get There One Raise at a Time

In your 30s, push the share of your pay you save for retirement toward 15%, counting any employer match, by adding half of every raise to your contribution. Keep most of that money in stocks, and don’t cut those contributions to pay for a house or the kids’ college.

Your 30s tend to bring bigger paychecks, and bigger costs competing for them: a down payment, child care, and a college fund. Saving for retirement is the easiest goal to shortchange, because no bill arrives when you skip it.

Fidelity suggests saving at least 15% of your pre-tax pay for retirement each year, counting what your employer adds. That rate assumes you start at 25 and retire at 67. If you start from nothing at 30, Fidelity’s target rises to 18%, and from 35 it’s 23%.

To see where you stand, compare your retirement savings with Fidelity’s benchmarks by age. They use the same assumptions and call for at least one year’s salary saved by 30 and three times your salary by 40.

Raises are the easiest time to save more, because half of each raise can go to retirement while your take-home pay still grows. On a 4% raise, that means contributing 2 more percentage points of your pay.

Say you’re 35 and earn $80,000. You put 8% of your pay into your 401(k), and your employer adds 3%. Raising your contribution from 8% to 12% invests an extra $3,200 a year and brings your total, match included, to 15%.

Then hold that rate when other goals compete. Put retirement ahead of the kids’ college. Build a down payment on top of your contributions, and keep it in savings, not stocks. Keep the retirement money itself mostly in stocks, since you won’t need it for decades. Add bonds only if you need them to sit through a steep drop without selling.

Before your next raise takes effect, log in to your plan’s website and add half of it to your contribution rate, so you never start spending that half.

#8426. Gifted Stock Carries Your Cost Basis – Give It to Someone in the 0% Bracket

The credit card, banking, and other financial offers that appear on this site are from companies that compensate us – for example, when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. To give stock, transfer the shares to the recipient’s brokerage account or a child’s custodial account. Your cost basis, what you paid, goes with them, so the recipient owes tax on your gain when they sell. Give appreciated shares to someone whose low income means 0% tax on long-term gains, and sell losing shares yourself to deduct the loss.

The gain you built is then taxed at the recipient’s rate, not yours, so the right recipient can owe nothing.

Say shares you bought years ago for $2,000 are worth $10,000 now, and you pay 15% on long-term gains, those on investments held over a year. Selling them yourself costs $1,200 in federal tax on the $8,000 gain.

Give them to your daughter in her first full year of work after college. The time you’ve held them counts as hers, so she gets long-term rates at once. If her taxable income, the gain included, stays low enough for the 0% long-term rate, she owes no federal tax on it. The kiddie tax limits this for anyone under 18, and for 18-year-olds and full-time students under 24 whose earnings cover no more than half their support. It taxes their investment income above a small yearly amount at a parent’s rate when that’s higher.

To make the gift, you’ll need the recipient’s brokerage name and account number for your broker’s online gift tool or form. For a child, open a custodial account, often called a UTMA or UGMA account, in their name. The shares become the child’s the day you give them, and the custodian manages them until the child comes of age.

Giving over $19,000 in a year to one person other than your spouse means filing a gift tax return, but you owe tax only once your lifetime gifts pass a multimillion-dollar exemption. Shares given to a charity or a donor-advised fund leave no one owing tax on the gain, since charities pay no income tax. Heirs who inherit shares in a taxable account get the shares’ value at death as their basis, so the gain before then goes untaxed.

Never give shares worth less than you paid. Neither of you can deduct the drop that came before the gift. Sell them, deduct the loss on your own return, and give the cash.

Before the transfer, open your broker’s cost basis page and send only the batches of shares that have gained.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

The “Never 100” rule and “Straight A” strategy have become cornerstones of my financial habits, helping me live below my means and automate my savings and giving. It was perfect for someone like myself who didn’t want a complicated, jargon-filled financial class – and wasn’t going to sign up for an intense ‘shame & blame’ session either.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Dylan is a devoted husband, father, and Christian leader who serves in lay-ministry at Calvary Chapel of Westmoreland County. With a background in marketing for influential organizations such as The Navigators ministry and Highmark Health, he brings a unique perspective to his passion for developing practical discipleship tools. He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.
