Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Log into your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. If you don't have 17,500 miles already, check your transferable points balances:

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

Let's walk through a real scenario that illustrates exactly what this redemption looks like in practice.

The Setup: You've just arrived at London Heathrow on a transatlantic award — perhaps an ANA First Class redemption through the very same Flying Club program. You have a few days in London, and now you need to get to Athens, Greece, where your Mediterranean adventure begins. You check flights: a business class seat on Virgin Atlantic's LHR → ATH route on your target date is priced at $2,200 cash.

The Redemption: You log into virginatlantic.com and find a business class award seat on that same flight: 17,500 Virgin miles + approximately $120 in taxes and fuel surcharges. You have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your ThankYou account from your Citi Premier card. You initiate the transfer — 1:1, instant — and within minutes, your Flying Club account reflects 17,500 miles (with 2,500 to spare for future use). You complete the booking.

The Experience: On the day of travel, you access the Virgin Clubhouse at Heathrow — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world. The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Do this: Search 331 days out for peak season Virgin's booking window opens exactly 331 days before departure. For summer travel to Athens, Rome, or other peak European destinations, business class award inventory gets claimed early. Set a phone reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date. Log in that morning. The seats that seem impossible to find in the 60-day window are often available the moment the calendar rolls over.

Do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. If you send 17,500 Chase points over and then discover the seat isn't actually available (or you misread the cabin class), those miles are stuck in Flying Club. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. They don't destroy the CPP math, but they're a genuine cash cost you need to plan around.

Do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

The ideal candidate is someone who's already planning a trip that routes through London Heathrow — perhaps on a transatlantic award — and needs an elegant, high-value way to reach their final European destination. Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. At 17,500 miles per person, a couple needs 35,000 Virgin miles, which is completely achievable with a single transfer from a combined Chase or Amex balance.

Families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. Multiplying 17,500 miles per person across four or more travelers creates a significant points requirement, and availability for multiple seats on the same flight is far from guaranteed. The fuel surcharges also multiply with passenger count. Families are better served by other redemption strategies.

This is NOT for beginners. The overall score of 2.7/5 and beginner-friendliness rating of 1/5 signal real complexity. If you're just starting your travel rewards journey, build your foundation with simpler redemptions first. But if you've got a year of points accumulation behind you and you're ready to think architecturally about trip planning, this sweet spot can be a revelatory experience.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally shows availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Log into VirginAtlantic.com and search for reward flights in Upper Class (business) on your desired European route. Look for VS-coded flights only. Ignore partner-operated results, which will price differently.

Midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

The Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.

#8411. Russian Team Moving Up on Everest

The only team currently on Everest has set off across an untouched Khumbu Icefall. There are no ladders or ropes at this time of year, and everything ahead of them is uncertain.

Earlier this week, the Russian team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina acclimatized toward the Nuptse shoulder, to the right of the Khumbu Icefall. Heavy snow slowed them, eventually forcing them to stop for the night at 5,650m.

Nuptse in the sun, with the Khumbu Glacier at the base and Everest’s West Shoulder on the left. Photo: Russian Everest Expedition 2026

Returning to their quarters in Lobuche, the team focused on rest and pondered their options. “We are considering two alternatives: either going up across the Khumbu Icefall or trying the West Ridge via the Lho La, the mountain pass to the left of the Khumbu Glacier that leads to Everest’s west ridge,” they said. Jost Kobusch has attempted the West Ride/Lho La route several times in winter.

The Russians have now chosen the first option. “We’re heading up, attempting to get through the Khumbu Icefall,” Vasilief told Mountainclub. “We’ll see how things go from there.”

The team plans to spend six days on the mountain and has not confirmed whether they will attempt the summit or complete another partial trip.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8410. Weekend Warm-Up: Sending Ivindo Falls

Gabon Uncharted: Sending Ivindo Falls follows a crew of young kayakers, as they attempt to paddle 150km down the Ivindo River’s many rapids, gorges, and waterfalls.

The four kayakers are what the film’s narrator calls the “top of the crop.” After taking a moment to admire this charming malaphor (I think our narrator has combined “cream of the crop” and “top of the class”) we meet the Send team. Leader Adrian Mattern of Germany spent years planning their trip to Gabon, bringing with him the talkative Dane Jackson, patient Kalob Grady, and Bren Orton. Orton signed on with the shiny-faced, inevitably short-lived optimism of a youngster in 1914 headed for the front, sure of being home by Christmas.

“Apparently,” the narrator notes, “no one told him what he was getting into on this trip.”

Once on the ground, they load up their supplies and set out on a long stretch of flat water. Struggling along behind, we meet the film crew, an interesting behind-the-scenes look at the process of filming a professional, well-funded adventure documentary. Filmmaker Olaf Obsommer, photographer David Sodomka, and narrator David Arnaud do everything the Send team does, backward and in heels. Or, no — I’m thinking of Ginger Rogers.

Obsommer was part of the first team to scout the river by kayak in 2007. They portaged past most of the rapids for safety. Nowadays, better kayaks and the ability to scout ahead by drone will, hopefully, let them complete what he started.

At the first of four whitewater sections, Kongou, they settle in to take the rocky labyrinth piece by piece. If they take the wrong branch, they’ll be heading over a 25m waterfall.

Adrian is entranced by Kongou Falls, and only when the team delicately sit him down and explain that he would very likely drown, which would be awkward, does he agree to move on. Photo: Screenshot

They work their way down the river looking for rapids that will not kill them immediately. On the way, they get advice from Juste Parfait Zangonga, a local expert, on how to not be killed by elephants, gorillas, crocodiles, vipers, or hippos.

The next rapids, Mingouli, are less maze, more rollercoaster. The Send team can finally start living up to their name. Between first descents, they paddle past a family of elephants and get devoured by insects.

First descent down a tricky section of Mingouli. Photo: Screenshot

Kouata Mango, section three, is where Mattern finally gets to send a massive waterfall. The team agrees that this one is less likely to kill him badly, and over the side he goes.

Tsengue Lelendi, the final set of rapids, rounds out the trip. The laconic Kaleb takes a look at one particularly rough section and tells our narrator that the rapid is unrunnable. The rest of the team spends a long time debating it, anyway. Lo and behold, he’s right. After scouting with drones, mapping every angle, and discussing the route at length, they agree to skip a section of the rapid. The chain will still have just a few missing links left.

“A part of this river will remain untouched,” Arnaud concludes, “as it should, probably.”

Red Bull doesn’t allow embeds, but you can watch the full film here.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8409. Upgrading To A Home You Don’t Need: A Three-Year Review

Toward the end of 2023, we upgraded to a larger finished home we didn't need. Three years later, I want to share whether it was worth it, so you can make a better decision if you're tempted to do the same.

More than any other material item money can buy, a home is the most desirable. The average person spends over 14 hours a day at home, so there's also probably no investment we use more. Sure, we have to wear clothes in public, but we swap them out every day. And last I checked, my t-shirts and shoes don't appreciate in value.

Fine watches and jewelry are nice and can appreciate too. But we don't wear them every day, and we definitely don't live inside them. So hands down, a home is the best combination of enjoying your money while also potentially making a positive return.

Upgrading to a home you don't need is a slightly different animal.

If you upgrade into something other people find undesirable or unnecessary, your home probably won't give you a positive return you're hoping for. But if you upgrade in the “frenzy zone” price range, the one buyers fight over in your market, you'll almost always have strong demand when it's your turn to sell.

My wife and I talked about this on our podcast, and we've concluded the purchase was worth it.

It took a tremendous amount of convincing to get her to agree to move. She finally acquiesced after I promised this would be our last house ever, assuming we stay in San Francisco. That promise was the main thing that got her over the line.

Our children have enjoyed the extra space tremendously. They play in the enclosed front yard every day, and we don't have to worry about them getting hit by a car or snatched by a stranger. The neighborhood is quiet and safe, although there's now a lot of remodeling going on.

I've also noticed our boy needs to run around more than our daughter, which seems typical. Once he's burned off the energy, it's easier to get him to focus on homework.

If you have a boy, or any extremely active child, a home on a large, usable lot can be beneficial for childhood development. That's something we didn't fully appreciate before buying.

There's also peace in knowing we'll never move again. For 20 years, from 2003 to 2023, I was addicted to real estate and constantly climbing the property ladder. Now that we've reached the top rung we can afford, I feel settled in a way I didn't expect. No more wanting feels amazing!

If you're focused on decumulation, or at least on spending more of the hard-earned money and risky investments that have paid off, it feels good to turn that money into something you actually enjoy.

A nicer home checks the box of being something we use every single day, which is more than I can say for most things I've spent on.

From a purely financial standpoint, the toughest part of upgrading to a home you don't need is thinking about how much more you could have made had you invested elsewhere, usually in stocks.

The S&P 500 is up over 80% since we sold stocks and Treasury bonds to buy our home. The opportunity cost of not making more elsewhere must be weighed against the utility you derived from your home.

It could always be worse, though. I talked to one dad who sold his Salesforce (CRM) stock in 2009 to buy his home. Had he held on, the stock would be up about 10X. I talked to another dad, currently thinking about upgrading, who worked at Tesla and sold shares in 2015 to buy his place. That stock is up more than 20X since.

Both of their properties are also up since purchase. But their old stock positions are up dramatically more.

All in, I'm sure I've left over $1 million on the table by buying our house, net of how much the house has appreciated. The opportunity cost could have been worse, but luckily the San Francisco housing market is strong thanks to AI. It's boom loop time.

I'm not sure we could buy our house today if it came on the market. In 24 years of searching for property in San Francisco, I've never seen a lot this size at this price point. So maybe the market is adjusting higher than I think, especially as the west side of San Francisco gets more popular.

The general recommendation is to set aside 1% of your home's value each year for maintenance. It's a decent rule of thumb, especially if you own a condo with a homeowners association, which I also do.

But after three years in the house, here's what we've actually spent:

That's roughly $4,700 over three years, or about $1,567 a year for pure maintenance. Practically nothing, and far below the 1% rule of thumb.

The low cost isn't entirely luck. We were thorough during the three-month escrow and had the sellers fix as much as possible before closing. The house had also been gut remodeled and fully landscaped right before our purchase, so we bought near the top of its maintenance cycle, not the bottom.

Run through this checklist before you fall in love and experience buyer’s remorse:

1) Make sure your spouse is genuinely on board. Not “fine, whatever” on board. Actually on board and extremely excited. A reluctant partner turns a great house into a recurring argument. Make a promise you can keep, like I did, and mean it.

2) Run the 30/30/3-5 rule. Have at least 30% of the purchase price saved (20% down, 10% buffer), keep the monthly payment under 30% of your gross income, and limit the home price to no more than 3 to 5 times your annual gross income. Break this rule and you invite stress.

3) Buy just above the frenzy zone. Pick a home and neighborhood that buyers fight over, then look for a price point about 10% higher. The frenzy zone is where most people bid, which means bidding wars that can leave you with tremendous buyer’s remorse if you win. Just above it, there’s less competition and better deals.

3) Stress test your cash flow. Model the new mortgage, property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, then assume one income disappears for six months. If the math gives you a panic attack, you’re stretching too far. I went through a six-month period of living paycheck to paycheck which recreated the stress I felt in banking almost every day.

4) Decide mortgage vs. cash with your opportunity cost in mind. Before you sell investments, ask what that money would likely earn if you left it alone, because that’s the cost you’ll feel most. Paying cash removes the monthly payment but concentrates your money in one illiquid asset. A mortgage keeps more invested but costs you fees, paperwork, and a lien.

If you can afford to pay cash and the home is worth 30% or less of your net worth after purchase, the cash route makes sense with interest rates this high. You can often get a better deal, or win the bid, by closing quickly with cash.

5) Hire an inspector and use a long escrow. This is where you create leverage. Find every defect and push the seller to fix as much as possible before closing. Our low maintenance bill is a direct result of being relentless during escrow.

6) Match the home to your family’s actual life. Active kids need a lot to run around on. Aging parents with bad hips prefer a single-story or a guest suite. Buy for how you’ll really live now and in the future, not for the staged photos, and not to impress people who aren’t paying your property tax bill.

In conclusion, we would happily buy this home again. The experience has worked out, but of course, it could easily have not. I cannot get these three years back, but I can appreciate how this house has provided a nicer life for my wife and children.

The one thing I might change is taking out a mortgage so I wouldn't have had to sell so much stock. But a mortgage would have cost about $10,000 in fees upfront, plus more work, plus the bank holding a lien. So maybe not.

Money is meant to be spent and enjoyed while we're still alive. So if you want to upgrade your home, go right ahead. Just follow the 30/30/3-5 rule so you don't put yourself in financial jeopardy and end up too stressed to enjoy the place.

Readers, have you ever upgraded to a home you didn't need? Was it worth it, or do you wish you'd kept the money invested? And if you're on the fence right now, what's holding you back?

Upgrading our home concentrated a big chunk of our net worth in one illiquid asset on one street in one city. Great for the kids. Not great for diversification.

If you want more real estate exposure without selling stocks, fixing fence planks, or paying a plumber at 10pm, take a look at Fundrise. AI may be the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs a physical home. Hyperscalers are pouring hundreds of billions a year into data centers, and power and permitting have become the binding constraint. Real estate is where that constraint gets solved.

Fundrise lets you invest in private real estate passively, with a low minimum. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai, and our investment philosophies are aligned.

My wife and I recorded a podcast episode looking back on our first three years in the house as well, including whether she’s forgiven me for convincing her to move. It's also a great discussion about life after FIRE, parenthood, and tackling growing desires. Listen on Apple or Spotify.

We recently upgraded our home into my “stretch” zone. We lived in our previous home for 13 years with the intent on keeping it as a rental, +3x the value and low 30 year mortgage

When our new house came up in January this year there was a bidding war and we won. I’m confident it could have gone higher but the seller only wanted to market it for 5 days. We put down 31.5% on the purchase with a 7 year I/O at 5.25%.

I’ve felt a lot of stress when I think of the big picture because I’m somewhat risk adverse. We kept our house with a great tenant for two years that exceeded my rent expectations.

When I get overwhelmed, I step back and take a hot tub (private gate into association pool/hot tub) and look around and realize I’ve upgraded my family to one of the nicest best run beach cities in SoCal. They aren’t making more land, the house brings immense joy to me and my family. We are off the busy street we lived in before and it’s so much more peaceful, safer.

I’ve reached deep into AI to help when I get stressed and it validates the purchase math, my investment thesis, and my belief in the area we invested.

While my business has been down, 100% commission, in the end of the day I realize much of my stress is my mind playing tricks one me by playing out worst case scenarios. The psychology of making life changing big moves is really something else. In a few years, I’ll be more comfortable as I grow into our new reality. Buffet always talks about the psychology of investing and it’s a real doozy.

Yes indeed. The stress of making big investment decisions can really get to you.

In three years, your home should feel much more affordable. Hope you can enjoy it as much as possible.

Sam, Would you watch or update the “30% of your net worth” home purchase rule to reflect home value as it appreciates? Suppose your purchase fits well within that rule at first, but doubles (hey, it could happen) in only a couple years. Now you have significant equity but also very high taxes, insurance, and perhaps even higher maintenance costs. How does that square?

If the home itself surges in value much faster than your overall net worth growth, then it’s just a reason to feel great about your purchase. There’s no need to sell it and buy a new house to get it down to 30% or lower. Enjoy the great purchase and the good times.

The extra cost should be affordable if you bought anywhere near the other two variables.

Regarding the 30/30/3-5 rules, it seems that it’s dependent on income. In other words, a 100K income on 500K home and small down payment vs 500K income with large down payment on 2.5M home looks a lot different. If coming in with a large down payment, that would seemingly impact the 3-5Xs income rule quite a bit vs 3-5Xs the entire purchase price?

Scenarios: 500K income 2.65M purchase price 1.275M down payment 1.375M mortgage

It’s a general guideline to hit within the ranges of the three variables.

The down payment variable is more powerful, where if you put a larger down payment down, you can do a higher multiple of income.

The down payment is more certain, but the income variable can change at any moment.

Figured. Ok, looking to upgrade to a home we don’t need that has quite a few scarcity features that aren’t easy to replicate, so likely a now or never scenario.

It is surprising how fast three years have passed by. We bought a house four years ago with cash, and I am nodding my head in agreement with each of your points. If I had kept the home purchase money invested in Apple, that stock’s value would have doubled. I am reminded of Charlie Munger’s quote, “The first rule of compounding: Never interrupt it unnecessarily.”

Also, the home purchase price pushed up against your “30% or less of net worth” rule.

Neither of these issues have created financial stress in our lives, and we own a very nice house. And, if this home turns into our “forever home” I will also have a “forever job” of fixing things. LOL

That’s great things have worked out. And mainly it’s probably because you spent reasonably, and within my guidelines.

Getting to the point of buying too much house, over five times you’re gross income, and hoping your job will continue to be there and your income will continue to grow is very risky proposition in this market.

What a fun recap and glad to hear it’s worked out well for your family. Any relocation, even if it’s just from one street to the next around the corner, is a big commitment of time, energy, and often higher cost. Any major change is always a risk so that’s great it was worth it for you. There’s also something incredibly priceless about feeling settled and not having to move again. Enjoy your home!

“Now that we’ve reached the top rung we can afford…” If one of your AI investments goes to the moon, you might be able to afford a lot more. On a related note, where do you see the top of the frenzy zone in SF?

#8408. Dhaulagiri: Rope Fixing Halted For Unclear Reasons

About 20 climbers from several teams had planned to start their summit push on Dhaulagiri today, and conditions couldn’t be better: bluebird skies, low wind, and setting snow. So why are climbers stuck at Camp 2? And why are they so angry?

“We are…stuck here at Camp 2 waiting for the route above us to be fixed,” Paul Clarke of Australia texted to ExplorersWeb this morning.

As Clarke explained, the Sherpa team from Seven Summit Treks assigned to fix the route on Dhaulagiri this year refuses to lay ropes on the last sections above Camp 3.

“From what we are being told here at Camp 2, SST’s VVIP clients are no longer planning to climb higher,” Clarke said. “As a result, the company has little motivation to continue fixing the route for the remaining climbers.

The rope-fixing team had laid ropes until some 400m above Camp 3 earlier last week. The SST leader, Makalu Sherpa, shared his latest update on Friday. At that time, he reported everything was going well. The rope-fixing team made good progress while the clients waited at Camp 2. Neither SST nor 14 Peaks Expeditions has updated about Dhaulagiri since then. There have been no safety concerns reported during the current push.

In recent years, 8,000m peaks have been fixed either by a dedicated team assigned by the Expedition Operators Association of Nepal or by agreement among the companies on the mountain. They assign the rope fixing to a team of volunteers, whom the other operators all chip in to pay. Most 8,000m clients these days lack the skills to climb on their own and depend entirely on fixed ropes (and a packed trail) prepared by Sherpas.

The assigned rope-fixing team may stop for safety reasons, such as bad weather or risky conditions. We are waiting for further statements to clarify the situation. For now, unless a different group of Sherpas takes over, there will be no summit push.

This has frustrated those like Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha of Hungary. The pair patiently remained at Base Camp during the storm two weeks ago and have been at Camp 2 for five days, waiting for their moment. It’s mid-October, and there will probably be no further opportunities for them.

Today, Anni Penttila of Finland posted a text in Finnish on Instagram that translates to:

“Nothing came of it this time, either. It’s so disappointing that there’s really nothing to say at this point. Everyone turned back to Base Camp today.”

Anni Penttila’s story today from Dhaulagiri.

As the clients all retreat, Andrzej Bargiel remains at Base Camp with his large support and film team. The Polish skier intends to climb and ski down Dhaulagiri without oxygen. He has already skied eight other 8,000m peaks in that style, including Everest.

#8407. Kyrgyz Climb 'Eternal Flame' Route on Nameless Tower

On September 28, a Kyrgyz team made its country’s first ascent of 6,239m Nameless Tower.

The expedition was led by Mikhail Mikhailov, known for his role in the 2004 North Face ascent of Jannu, which earned a Piolet d’Or, and for the 2009 first ascent of Peak 6134 on Minya Konka with Alexander Ruchkin, according to Mountain.ru.

Other members of the Nameless Tower group include Mikhail Danichkin, Timur Akbashev, Aidar Akbashev, Zarina Kutanova, and Aleksei Pototsky. The Kyrgyz team carried out the technical climb of this soaring granite spire, one of the Trango Towers, via the famous Eternal Flame route.

Nameless Tower. Photo: Timur Akbashev/Mountain.ru

Eternal Flame is one of the most celebrated big-wall routes in the Karakoram. It was first climbed in September 1989 by Kurt Albert, Wolfgang Gullich, Christof Stiegler, and Milan Sykora on Nameless Tower’s South Face. The original climbing route is roughly 650m long, on a vertical wall with a total height of about 1,000m. It was graded VI, 7b+, A2.

The route combines sustained hard granite climbing with the altitude, logistics, and objective hazards of a 6,000m Karakoram peak, which is why it has remained a major objective for both free climbers and traditional alpinists. The Kyrgyz ascent adds its country’s name to the short list of teams that have summited by this classic line.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8406. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Adventure Has No Retirement Age: Adventure is continuing well into the ninth decade of life for a growing number of paddlers and hikers. Ninety-one-year-old Dale “Greybeard” Sanders only took up extreme endurance challenges at 80. Since then, he has paddled the Mississippi River from source to sea twice, completed the Missouri River Race, and this year reclaimed the record as the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail.

The challenge of competing and breaking records keeps him going, but not everyone is chasing endurance records. For Wendy Eden, 77, the goal is just to be out in nature and to keep exploring her beloved Canadian wilderness on her own. That means adapting her approach as she gets older.

I Hitchhiked From Sydney to Perth: Aston Brown describes his experience of hitchhiking across Australia from Sydney to Perth. He sees hitchhiking as an opportunity to surrender control and connect with people he would otherwise never meet.

Far more common in the 1970s and 1980s, the practice plummeted in Australia because of its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who targeted hitchhikers. Now it is starting to pick up again, as online communities and social media introduce it to a new generation.

Brown recognizes that hitchhiking carries dangers and that his experience as a man does not reflect the risks women traveling alone face. Yet his journey left him with a sense of connection. He spent three days and 1,900km traveling with Neil, a 79-year-old widower, on a four-month road trip around Australia. He also met a Zimbabwean family who had left the U.S. because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns, a retired tractor enthusiast, and Doug, head of Australia’s national science agency, who invited him birdwatching to see one of the country’s rarest birds.

She Had a Will To Live: A 72-year-old hiker survived six nights in the wilderness after falling 30m down a steep embankment. Mary Beth Granbery was on the Cabin Creek Trail near Mount Shasta in California when she fell.

She had set out on a multi-day camping trip and was expected home within four days. When she failed to return, friends and family raised the alarm. Rescuers found her camper van at the trailhead and launched a search. They found her one day later, at the bottom of the embankment. Despite suffering injuries from the fall, dehydration, and hypothermia from the cool nights, Granbery was still conscious when the rescue team reached her.

Across Madagascar To Find The World’s Last Lemurs: Geena Truman and her husband took a 2,500km road trip across Madagascar to search for lemurs. In a rented 4×4, they set off from Antananarivo. On the RN7 highway, they drove through rainforest, highland rice paddies, canyons, and desert, encountering rare species including golden bamboo lemurs, ring-tailed lemurs, and Verreaux’s sifakas.

Leaving the highway, they ended up on rough tracks with tricky river crossings, mud pits, and routes so difficult to navigate that they hired a local guide, known as a pisteur, to find their way.

Driving through Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees towards Tsingy de Bemaraha and Kirindy Reserve. Photo: Geena Truman

Grand Ole Roadtrip: In the summer of 1976, six young climbers piled into a blue Ford van and drove west to tackle Wyoming’s Teton Range. That first trip to the Tetons saw them face loose rock on the Enclosure Ice Couloir, a terrifying slide down the Skillet Couloir that nearly carried two of the group over a glacier’s edge, and two separate encounters with violent thunderstorms that left them clinging to exposed rock.

At the heart of all of this was the Grand Teton Climbers’ Ranch (GTRC), an affordable base for mountaineers. It offered more than a cheap bed: It was a place to meet climbing partners, exchange stories, and recover from the day over shared meals. Today, the GTRC remains one of their favorite places on Earth.

Renate Powell Completes Munro Round in Barefoot Shoes: Renate Powell has completed her second round of Scotland’s 282 Munros, this time in barefoot shoes. The keen hillwalker turned to minimalist footwear in her forties when an old skiing injury left her knee in constant pain.

She started by walking just 100m a day, then spent more than a year gradually building up to take on a Munro in her barefoot shoes. Fourteen years after first trying them, she continues her long-distance walking, without the knee replacement that was initially suggested.

Climbing the Cuillin Munro in barefoot shoes. Photo: Gillian Parker

Mad, Bad and Dangerous To Know: Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, has been living with Parkinson’s for seven years. He’s been out of the public eye for two years, and his current state is uncertain.

Fiennes spent much of his life building a remarkable expedition career after serving in the military. His 1979-82 Transglobe Expedition saw him and fellow former SAS soldiers Charles Burton and Oliver Shepard complete a 60,000km circumnavigation using surface travel, crossing both Poles.

He later completed a 2,170km unsupported ski crossing of Antarctica with Mike Stroud, and attempted to reach the North Pole unsupported five times. After severe frostbite during a 2000 expedition, he famously amputated his own dead fingertips with a fretsaw. This article plots out the timeline of his extraordinary expeditions.

A Climber Has Now Called For Help Three Times in 2026: Two climbers had to be rescued on September 22 after becoming stranded on the 500m White Dyke scramble on British Columbia’s Edge Peak. The pair set out at 8:30 am, but later that afternoon, with only three hours until sunset, the less experienced climber was too exhausted to continue.

After two hours attempting to rescue themselves, they activated a Garmin SOS beacon. This is the third time one of the climbers in the duo has had to be rescued this year. Rescue veteran Brent Boulet warned that social media seems to be drawing less experienced people onto technical routes. He stressed the importance of realistic timing, turning back when necessary, and knowing a climbing partner’s capabilities before setting out.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8405. Controversy Continues on Dhaulagiri as Expeditions Called Off

After Manaslu, Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er this season with no summits. The rope-fixing team says they stopped working for safety reasons, but some climbers suspect other motivations and describe a tense atmosphere.

Paul Clarke of Australia — who had been waiting at Camp 2 for five days — shared his frustrations with ExplorersWeb. Clarke had just learned that the rope fixers had stopped working above Camp 3 and were retreating. He described a lack of motivation among the Sherpa rope fixers after VIP clients with Seven Summit Treks, the company in charge of fixing the route, had called off their summit attempt. Soon after, all 20 climbers waiting at Camp 2 were told to return to Base Camp.

“Makalu Lakpa came through the lower camp this morning after the decision had been made,” Clarke said. “It was a pretty uncomfortable atmosphere, and I think everyone understands just how badly this has affected the rest of the teams on the mountain.”

Clarke’s outfitter, 8K Expeditions, sent a Sherpa team to retrieve their gear and tents from Camp 3 at 7,100m.

A helicopter lands at Dhaulagiri Base Camp. Photo: Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

Makalu Lakpa Sherpa is leading the 14 Peaks Dhaulagiri Expedition, one of the two largest teams, together with its sister company, Seven Summit Treks. Today, he posted a message explaining that increasing winds on October 10 resulted in a higher risk of slab avalanches on October 11, when his team was due to attempt the summit. He says that is the only reason his team returned to Base Camp.

In an unusual remark, Lakpa stated that he looks after his own group and cannot be held responsible for “other teams’ summit ambitions, climbing strategies, or rope-fixing arrangements.” He also noted that the rope-fixing work was assigned to Seven Summit Treks, not his team.

Finally, he spoke out against climbers who had expressed their disagreement yesterday:

To those criticizing our decision from a distance, I ask you to understand the actual mountain conditions before passing judgment. Assessing risks firsthand and making decisions that determine whether a team returns home safely is very different from commenting on social media.

Guides working for Lakpa’s company and for Seven Summit Treks have posted messages on social media supporting his decision. Benny Lieber, an American guide working for 14 Peaks, posted his assessment of avalanche risks on the mountain:

A post on Dhaulagiri conditions by Benny Lieber on Instagram. Photo: Benny Lieber/Instagram

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, leader of Seven Summit Treks, argued that the weather window was too short, given that a summit push would take “several days.” The plan was to move up to Camp 3 on October 11, reach the summit on the morning of October 12 (with October 13 as a buffer day), and return to Base Camp the following day.

Chhang Dawa, a director at Seven Summit Treks, posted about Dhaulagiri’s weather forecasts. Photo: Chhang Dawa/Instagram

Still, these explanations have not satisfied some climbers. Their biggest frustration came from watching the mountain in perfect, windless weather (though a wind plume eventually grew on the summit, according to Benny Lieber).

“From my perspective, one of the biggest frustrations is how badly the weather window appears to have been misread by Makalu Sherpa,” Paul Clarke said. “The strong winds and poor climbing conditions yesterday were not a surprise, since we had all been watching the forecasts for days, and winds in the 40–50kph range had been clearly visible well in advance.

“Despite that, Makalu Sherpa sent the rope-fixing team and his VIP clients higher on the mountain yesterday in conditions that were obviously going to be difficult. That has left climbers from multiple other operators stranded by a decision they had no control over. The consequence is that the rope-fixing team has now come back down, the VIP clients are no longer continuing [a helicopter was waiting for them as they arrived in Base Camp], and we have just been told that all our expeditions are over.”

Vincere Zeng of Singapore also shared her pòint of view with ExplorersWeb. Zeng has summited seven 8,000’ers, and was the first Singaporean woman to summit K2 and Annapurna. “I attempted it [Dhaulagiri] last autumn as well, so I was fully aware of the risks involved, which is why I had been monitoring the weather closely every day,” she said.

Zeng explained that her group was aware of high winds on October 9 and 10, and therefore waited at Camp 2. They planned to attempt the summit today, on October 12, in the morning. “We also considered Oct 12-13 as a possible buffer, as the next strong wind cycle was forecast to arrive around the afternoon of Oct 14,” Zeng explained.

“What I did not understand was why the 14 Peaks team chose to move toward Camp 3 (~7,000m) on Oct 10, which was the windiest day in the forecast, and then cancelled the rope fixing based on the conditions they encountered that day,” Zeng said. “From our side, we hoped we would at least have the opportunity to assess conditions during the originally planned Oct 11-12 window.”

Both Clarke and Zeng said that the 8K Sherpas who went to Camp 3 yesterday to retrieve equipment reported good conditions to that point.

“Of course, that does not mean conditions higher up, particularly around the traverse and summit slopes, were necessarily safe,” Zeng noted. “But it was one reason I hoped conditions could be reassessed once the forecasted wind had passed, especially as we still had time to do so. Instead, we were informed that the expedition was cancelled before we had that opportunity.”

Vincere Zeng (with green down suit) waits at Camp 2 in good weather last weekend. Photo: Vincere Zeng

Zeng explained she was “absolutely prepared to turn around if an assessment showed that conditions were unsafe.”

Clarke confirmed that all commercial expeditions on Dhaulagiri have called off their attempts. With the big teams pulling out, there is no manpower to launch another commercial-style attempt.

“At this point, nearly all of the teams have already packed up their Base Camp operations, and almost all of the climbers have flown out by helicopter, either yesterday afternoon or this morning,” Clarke said.

One team, however, has no intention of leaving. Andrzej Bargiel’s expedition, which includes a significant support team and film crew, is still hoping to summit and ski down the mountain, as he explained to fellow climber Xenia Santha of Hungary today.

“We wish Andrzej [Bargiel] the best of luck,” Clarke said. “If he can continue and summit, it will obviously provide another very clear picture of what the conditions on the mountain were actually like during this window.”

Risk assessment is always a tricky issue on commercial expeditions. Climbers pay large sums of money and expect every possible summit chance. It is often hard to explain when conditions are too risky, considering that factors include avalanche risks and wind, but also group sizes, the skills and endurance of guided climbers, complex logistics, and the disastrous consequences of a wrong decision.

However, in this instance, it is the lack of choices rather than the conditions that has frustrated climbers. Ironically, commercial expeditions on big mountains are more interdependent that ever, but communication between them, and sometimes with their clients, can be poor.

“As a client, I have no exact knowledge of the rope-fixing arrangement or collaboration agreed between the different outfitters,” Zeng said. “As we were a relatively small team with less manpower [8K Expeditions], we were to some extent dependent on the main rope-fixing team and whatever cooperation had been agreed between the operators. So, once the main fixing effort stopped, in practical terms it also affected our ability to continue.”

“Seven Summit Treks and Makalu Lakpa are now, from our perspective, trying to justify the decisions that were made by saying the weather was the reason they stopped,” Clarke concluded after reading the posts by Makalu Lakpa and Chhang Dawa today. “Based on the forecasts we had been watching for days, what we saw ourselves, and now the reports from climbers and Sherpas who were actually higher on the mountain, I simply don’t agree with that explanation.”

Large expedition operators sometimes react only when climbers openly share their experiences and thoughts, and their reaction is often to try to stop the dissemination of news from the mountains.

Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha, said media coverage had caused tension. Santha received a text message asking why she and Clarke had been speaking to the press. “I found that quite surprising; we have only spoken publicly about what we experienced firsthand and about decisions that directly affected our expedition,” Clarke said.

#8404. Pain And Penalty: Why A Dad Bod Challenge Works When Willpower Doesn’t

If you want to lose weight and gain muscle, join a dad bod or a mom bod challenge. The social pressure to hit your goals will be immense. And if you put a financial penalty for not meeting your goals by a certain date, you will be even more motivated to get fitter.

Since graduating from college in 1999, I've weighed between 164 and 173 pounds at 5'10” tall. I'm currently about 165 pounds, 45 days after the start of my Dad Bod Challenge. The lightest I weighed as an adult was about 153 pounds, which lasted all of one year before I gained the freshman 10+ pounds during college.

After college, my doctor also suggested I should be around 155-157 lbs to hit my ideal weight. So for over 25 years I've been telling myself I'd like to lose 10 pounds. And I've never succeeded, only coming close when I grew to 173 pounds during the first year of fatherhood in 2017, and then again during the first year of COVID. After both periods, I ended up losing about 7 pounds at most.

But after hearing about some fellow dads at my kids' school entering the Dad Bod Challenge and losing a ton of weight while also gaining muscle, I was impressed. This could finally be the impetus I was looking for to lose that stubborn 10 pounds!

Let me explain our setup, so you might be incentivized to create your own. After all, once you're financially on track, you should get physically on track as well.

There are actually 10 of us in the Dad Bod Challenge. Here are the conditions:

$5,000 might sound steep, or to some, it might not sound like much. But overall, the penalty needs to feel painful enough to motivate you to lift weights, exercise, and reduce food consumption. A $1,000 penalty would be enough to get me motivated, while another might need a $50,000 penalty.

$50,000 would be a scary number to lose, especially as cash strapped as I am. However, on the flip side, with such a high penalty, there is no way I wouldn't meet my goals.

Overall, we agreed that $5,000 was a high enough penalty. After about 45 days, the judge also offered dads the option to buy an extension for $500 a week, for up to four weeks. If a dad buys the extension and meets his objectives, he gets all his money back and doesn't have to pay the $5,000 penalty.

This lifeline was a great relief for me given my slower-than-expected progress. But I'm also reluctant to take it because I need PAIN AND PENALTY to keep me motivated.

If you think losing weight is hard, try losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time. Way harder.

Muscle needs protein and calories to grow. A calorie deficit, which is how you lose fat, starves your muscles of the fuel they need. So the two goals fight each other.

Losing weight on its own is relatively simple. Track what you eat and run a daily calorie deficit large enough to hit your fat-loss target by a certain date. You don’t have to do more. You just have to eat less. Exercise helps, but roughly 80% of weight loss comes from diet. And if you exercise too much, you might overeat.

Building lean mass, which is mostly muscle, requires lifting weights. And not casual lifting. You need to lift to failure, where you can’t squeeze out another rep or two. That usually means at least three sets of 8 to 12 reps, adding weight over time to discover what you can really do.

When I was young, piling on more plates was a fun challenge. Now my joints and tendons ache when I push to the max, and that’s when the injury risk spikes.

Fellow dads have torn biceps, triceps, and pecs, and thrown out their backs lifting. My 70-year-old uncle, who looks like He-Man, tore a shoulder muscle this year and needed surgery. He’s out for at least two months.

If I get seriously injured, I will most likely fail the dad bod challenge. To win, or at least not lose, every dad must hit both his fat-loss and lean-mass goals at the final scan concurrently. You can’t hit your muscle target two months in and then lose it during the final 45 days because you focused only on cutting.

Body recomposition is far harder than doing either one alone. And this is my first time doing it

I hadn’t regularly lifted weights in over 10 years before this challenge.

The reasons were mostly laziness and boredom. I also have a shoulder injury that’s nagged me for at least six years. During COVID, I couldn’t throw a softball overhand without pain, so I mostly played first base and occasionally third. I’d rather not have surgery.

My hope was that going from zero to one would produce big gains. But I needed to be careful. If I hurt myself further, I might not be able to lift at all.

For 45 days, I watched what I ate. I cut way back on sugar and carbs and loaded up on protein shakes and chicken. On top of playing tennis and pickleball three times a week for about 1.5 hours a session, I added 30 to 40 minutes of walking a day.

After all that, my DEXA scan showed I’d lost only 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean tissue. I expected at least 4 pounds of fat loss, so I was disappointed. But I’m pleased with the lean tissue gain.

The good news is I still have about two months to go.

Over the next two months, I need to gain another 1 pound of lean mass and lose 11 pounds of fat. That’s a net loss of 10 pounds, which would put me at about 156.5 pounds. But a DEXA scan can easily fluctuate by half a pound, so my safer target is 156 or less.

I haven’t been under 160 pounds in 26 years, but I’ve dreamed about it, just like how I've dreamt of buying a mansion in paradise. Then reality sets in and bludgeons my hopes into the ground.

Kei Nishikori, a pro tennis player I’ve followed, has played at around 155 pounds at 5'10”. If he can do it, so can I. Of course, he’s a professional athlete who works out five hours a day and I’m a 49-year-old dad who writes. Still, I accepted the challenge.

As a tennis and pickleball player, I want to be lean. Big muscles are nice, but they slow down my speed and hands. It’s one reason you don’t see muscular players on the pro tour. To each their own.

The best part of a Dad Bod Challenge is the group. Everybody is supportive and brings a different nutrition and fitness background. We cheer each other on and answer each other’s questions. Although, some remain completely silent.

I don’t think anybody is primarily motivated by winning the other dads’ money. Everybody seems motivated by the chance to improve their health.

What’s interesting is that the goals aren’t uniform. We entered knowing the penalty and our own targets, but once the challenge started, we could see everyone else’s.

The judges tried to set fair goals and meet each dad where he was. But after seeing all the numbers, I probably should have negotiated a smaller fat-loss target.

For example, my buddy is two inches shorter than me and started 38 pounds heavier. He has to get down to about 196 pounds while I have to get down to 156 pounds. Our body compositions are different, as he has more lean mass, but losing a similar percentage of fat when you have less of it is harder.

That's life. Which brings me to the lessons a Dad Bod Challenge teaches about money and life.

Getting ripped and wealthy doesn't just happen. You've got to make it happen. Nobody is coming to save you.

The only reason I exercise is because tennis, pickleball, and softball are fun. If they weren’t, I wouldn’t. I don’t run for fun. I don’t walk for fun, although I do enjoy a nice hike.

This lack of fun is the main reason I stopped lifting weights. If I’m going to lift something heavy, I want to be productive, like hauling rocks and bags of mulch for a landscaping project. Curling a dumbbell in a gym felt pointless.

A Dad Bod Challenge forces discipline when fun isn’t enough. It gets you out the door for a 6 am run before work, or to the gym at 9 pm once the kids are in bed. The challenge also helps you get used to that throbbing feeling of hunger, which may make you more appreciative of the things you have.

Make the challenge long enough, 100 to 180 days, and the discipline compounds until it becomes part of your weekly routine.

Building wealth requires the same consistency. You need the discipline to save as much of each paycheck as possible, and the courage to put those savings at risk. Historically, stocks have gone up in roughly 70% of years. That’s when you feel great about your efforts, like losing fat and gaining muscle. The other 30% of the time, you lose a little or a lot and curse your timing, like getting injured.

Stick with both routines for 10 years and you’ll be blown away by the results. But staying disciplined for that long is hard. That’s where a workout buddy more gung-ho than you helps. It’s also where an automatic 401(k) contribution from every paycheck and an AI investment advisor helps.

Some people are born to wealthy, loving parents. Others are born into poverty, given up for adoption, or lose their parents as babies. Some people befriend the founders of a hot AI company and join before it hits it big. Others join startup after startup that goes bust.

The body is similar. Some people are born with fast metabolisms and uncanny strength. Others pack on weight despite working out constantly. Tall, skinny people may struggle to add muscle. Shorter, stockier people may bulk up with ease.

At 49, I'm one of the oldest dads in the group. The youngest is 39. Ah, I remember 39. I was five years into FIRE, traveling the world, and recovering much faster than I do now. I also didn’t have my shoulder and knee injuries. But the challenge gives older dads no handicap. No easier fat-loss targets, no lower lean-mass goals, no extra free time.

Compare your goals to someone else’s and you might get annoyed, because you have completely different genetics. The judges try to set fair goals, but they won’t get it perfect every time.

We can’t control the hand we’re dealt. We can only control our effort and attitude. So compare your progress to your old self and nobody else. If you hit your own goals, you won’t lose. If you happen to win some money too, great. The money was never the point.

What I love about my Dad Bod Challenge is that the creators and judges are fitness fanatics. They’re smart, enthusiastic, kind, and extremely fit. They’ve experienced the benefits of being in shape, so they’re paying it forward by organizing a challenge for 10 dads who are nowhere near as fit.

I’ve learned a ton about how to train, what to eat, how to recover, and how to supplement with protein. One example: spread your protein out, eating about 20 to 25 grams every few hours instead of cramming it all into one meal for better utilization.

Oh, and did you know a tablespoon of olive oil is around 120-140 calories?! Nuts!

I also lost all my excuses. I used to tell myself only people without kids or demanding jobs could get extremely fit. But the judges are dads and successful entrepreneurs. Excuses gone.

Paying it forward is also why I’ve published three times a week on Financial Samurai for over 17 years. No courses, no paywalls, just free content based on my experiences to help you reach financial freedom sooner. When I find a great strategy, like negotiating a severance if you plan on quitting anyway, I find it impossible not to share it.

Before this challenge, I had never measured my lean mass. I just stepped on a scale. But a scale lies by omission. You could lose two pounds of muscle and think you’re making progress. That's no good, especially for folks over 40 who begin to lose muscle more rapidly.

The DEXA scan showed me the truth. After 45 days, I’d lost 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean body mass. The scale only showed a 1.2-pound difference, which would have been demoralizing. The DEXA showed real recomposition, but also still a bummer because I thought I would have made greater gains.

Finances work the same way. Plenty of people only look at their income or checking account balance and think they’re doing fine. But income is just the scale. Net worth is the DEXA scan. It shows whether you’re building assets or just shuffling money around while debt quietly piles up.

I’ve tracked my net worth since 1999 and it’s one of the best financial habits I’ve ever built. Whatever you measure regularly, you naturally start to improve.

Empower is what I use to track my net worth once I moved on from spreadsheets in 2012. Mezzi is what I use to track my public investments and gain powerful financial insights to better optimize my portfolio.

At the end of the day, I want to build muscle and lose fat to increase my chances of living a longer, healthier life.

That’s primarily why I think more people should join a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you miss your exact targets, you’ll likely finish in better shape than when you started.

In high school and college, I stayed in shape to have the widest dating pool possible. My four years at William & Mary were a blast.

Once I started working, good dieting and regular exercise went out the window. During my first five years, staying under 170 pounds was a struggle. Eventually I settled into the mid-160s, playing competitive USTA tennis for 10 years and wanting every edge I could get.

Now, I want as much energy as possible to play with my kids. And I want to live long enough to meet my grandchildren.

So if you need a reason to get in shape and change your body composition, organize a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you lose, you’ll probably make new friends and end up fitter.

Here’s to greater strength and 156 pounds or less by December 23, 2026. More importantly, here’s to a lifetime of healthier habits going forward.

Readers, have you ever joined a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge with real money on the line? How big does a financial penalty need to be before it actually changes your behavior, $500, $5,000, or $50,000?

Life insurers notice when you get in shape. Your weight and health history help determine your health class, which drives your premiums. I had my first child two months before turning 40, so my kids will depend on me well into my 60s. Term life insurance is the cheapest way to make sure they’re OK if I don’t make it to grandparent duty.

If you have dependents, check out Policygenius. You can compare quotes from multiple top insurers in one place instead of calling around. The best time to lock in a policy is while you’re young and healthy. The second best time is right after you finish a Dad Bod Challenge. Both my wife and I got matching 20-year term life insurance policies with Policygenius and we feel mentally great as a result.

#8403. A Human-Powered Journey Around Norway

Bad weather has forced Norwegian Jonas Holm, 27, to alter his 5,500km human-powered attempt to circle Norway.

Holm took a year off from his construction job and set out from southern Norway in late April, beginning in Svinesund on the Swedish border. He planned to paddle nearly 3,000km north, skirting Norway’s coastline as far as Grense Jakobselv, near the Russian border. From there, he would travel south through Norway, Finland, and Sweden with his dog, Rago.

Jonas Holm during the kayak section of his journey. Photo: Jonas Holm/Padling

However, difficult conditions forced him to stop paddling south of Bodø in northern Norway, a little over halfway to Grense Jakobselv. On his website, Holm says he wants to avoid feeling pressure to reach particular places by particular dates, instead focusing on experiencing the landscape. With constant wind and rain, he decided the remaining fiords could wait until next spring.

Holm’s tracked route so far. Photo: Jonas Holm

Holm won’t sit on the couch until he can complete the coastline. Rather than wait months for better weather, he has stored his kayak and will begin the second segment of his journey: the 2,500km trek south from Grense Jakobselv. After a quick break at home to dry his clothes and gear, Holm recently drove north to Grense Jakobselv and set out with a backpack and a companion. Rago, his Alaskan malamute, is even carrying some equipment. As winter arrives and snow accumulates, Holm plans to eventually transition from walking with a backpack to skis and a pulk.

His exact route is unclear, but he will roughly trace Norway’s eastern border, though he mentions crossing parts of Finland and Sweden on his way back to his starting point in southern Norway.

You can follow Holm’s progress through the live tracker on his expedition website.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8402. New Flash Floods Disrupt Trekking Routes in Nepal

A flash flood has cut off parts of the Manaslu Circuit in a fresh blow to Nepal’s tourism industry.

This time, the flood hit the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. While not as catastrophic as the glacial lake outburst flood in the Langtang Lirung area in late August, the flooding is still severe. A landslide caused the river to swell suddenly, washing away houses and bridges and damaging a hydropower plant, the BBC reported. Authorities have not recorded any fatalities, but some farmers remain unaccounted for.

The Bhudi Gandaki River flows south from mountains in the Manaslu region, and the flood severed the popular Manaslu Circuit in several sections. The Chum Valley is currently isolated after bridges were washed away. According to the Manaslu Conservation Area Project (MCAP), all trekkers in the area are fine. The Tourism Times reports that helicopters are airlifting some tourists back to Kathmandu.

“We have decided to cancel our Manaslu and Tsum treks for this autumn season based on advice from local authorities and our internal risk assessments,” Roland Hunter of The Mountain Company told ExplorersWeb. Instead, they are offering clients a trek through Upper Mustang followed by a crossing of Thorong La, the highest point on the Annapurna Circuit.

Poor weather also closed Thorong La for weeks after a snowy spell hit Nepal’s mountains. However, the trail recently reopened, and trekking groups have crossed the pass over the last five days. “There is a trail through the snow on the pass, and after sunny weather the snow has consolidated, reducing the risk of avalanche,” Hunter explained. “The road has been washed away lower down near Chame, although the trekking trail has been repaired so it is passable for trekking groups.”

Hunter said that many trekkers are now diverting to the Annapurna Circuit, and he presumes it will be busier than ever for the next few weeks.

The Tourism Times also reports damaged trails on the Tashi Lapcha Pass, a high-altitude trekking route connecting the Rolwaling and Khumbu regions. Tashi Lapcha is one of the most challenging sections of the Great Himalaya Trail (GHT) and includes rock scrambling and fixed ropes that are currently damaged. The paper shared a report from IAM Trekking Guides:

The damaged section lies along the approach to the David Lama Bivouac shelter at Upper Jabo. Trekkers and climbers must use the fixed ropes and carefully scramble across the rocky terrain to proceed. The loss of footholds in such a steep section can increase the risk of a fall, particularly for groups carrying trekking or climbing equipment.

A damaged passage at Tashi Lapcha. Photo: IAM Trekking Guides

Those intending to hike in the area should ask their local trekking operators and tourism offices for updated information. According to India’s weather services, the monsoon officially left Nepal yesterday. Nepal’s peak trekking season begins now and lasts until the end of November.

#8401. Animal Attack Roundup

We usually hear about animal attacks that happen to hikers, tourists, and other visitors to an area. But it shouldn’t be surprising that most victims are the villagers who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here is a brief summary of the incidents worldwide in the last few days.

Hippo sinks family canoe, killing three — DR Congo

A family canoe on Lake Tumba. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

A mother and two of her children died when a hippopotamus reportedly rammed their wooden canoe during a nighttime crossing of Lake Tumba. Four family members were aboard; only one survived.

Mary Thandi, 35, and her 15-year-old daughter Esther suffered serious abdominal injuries when a hippopotamus attacked them near the Thiba River in the early evening of October 10.

They were returning home with two other people, who escaped. Both victims were hospitalized. Their current condition is unknown.

George Mbae Kalubira, 60, was fatally injured after encountering a wild elephant while searching for pasture for his goats around 5 am.

A snake catcher (not the one in this story) with a cobra. Photo: Shutterstock

A snake catcher died after being bitten in southern India. Initial reports in local press did not mention the snake species or how the bite occurred.

Police said the boars initially attacked the people at the front of the group, then charged the others. The three surviving victims suffered minor injuries.

Ishu Kumar, five, was reportedly bitten on a finger near a hand pump at a local childcare center. His family alleges that staff failed to arrange immediate medical treatment and sent him home. Neighbors later advised taking him for a ritual treatment, but he died.

Angry villagers then blocked a highway with the child’s body, demanding an investigation.

Charlette Gonsalves, 51, was bitten by a venomous snake in her kitchen early one morning before sunrise. Her family initially did not recognize the injury as a snakebite.

She was transferred between three hospitals as her condition deteriorated, but died the following morning.

A 44-year-old man was cutting grass near a pond in Đồng Tháp Province when a green snake bit his hand.

According to Vietnamese reporting, he became dizzy within three minutes and began vomiting blood approximately 20 minutes after the bite. He developed serious blood-clotting abnormalities and swelling extending toward his elbow.

Doctors administered antivenom and plasma. He survived.

The victim began vomiting, lost consciousness, and developed severe cardiovascular and neurological complications. He died approximately 83 hours after the bite.

#8400. Jordanian Man Trekking 23,000Km From South Africa to Siberia

Saddam Al Alaya is almost a year into his attempt to walk 23,000km from Cape Town, South Africa, to Magadan, in Russia’s Far East. The 35-year-old Jordanian left Cape Town on January 1, 2026, on a trek that he estimates will take three years. He covered the 5,500km to Rwanda in nine months, so he is on schedule.

This year, Al Alaya has already passed through South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Tanzania, Burundi, and now Rwanda. He expects to transit 18 countries in all, including his home country of Jordan, which he will cross from south to north.

Al Alaya grew up in Wadi Musa, beside Petra, and began guiding tourists around the famous archaeological site and the nearby canyons when he was about 16. He continued to guide while working for a business degree. He conceived the idea for this long walk in 2021, and spent almost five years organizing it.

Al Alaya meets a supporter. Photo: Facebook

Like so many adventurers, he wants to give his project a social angle, but Al Alaya seems particularly good at this. He founded an organization called Hike With Me, and many of his social media images show him glad-handing officials, walking with local people, or visiting regional schools. He often carries a white flag, symbolizing peace.

Al Alaya has official sponsorship from several Jordanian ministries, national organizations, and Jordanian embassies in various countries along the way. These have helped him with visas, security, and logistical support, according to the Jordanian News Agency.

Meeting some local people. Photo: Saddam Al Alaya
